options.title: One list, every room
options.line: One list of every room, always in the same order, each row saying whether the room is free and until when, answers her question the way the wall chart does: by where she looks, not by anything she does.

options.title: Free rooms first
options.line: Free rooms in a leading region of their own, each with its own Book action, do the filtering she would never do herself and put a walk-in two clicks away.

options.title: The day as a grid
options.line: A grid of rooms against the hours of the day, with a line at now, shows what is free now and what frees up next in the same glance.

seats.line: On B and on A she can place a walk-in without help; on C she has to find one thin column before she can answer.
All three show only what the product holds: the status of each room, when a booking ends and when the next one starts.
B says what is free now before anything else, which is what a front desk checks before it sends anyone.
She named a free room at a glance on B, read down the rows on A, and gave up on C.
She found the room on A first, because every room is always in the same place.

recommendation.reason: The usability judge, the profile judge and the primary reader each put B first, and the contrast reader put it second.

question: Which structure goes on to Detail: A, B or C?
